questions.question: Why is implementing Runnable preferred over extending Thread in Java?
questions.title: Runnable Preferred Over Thread Extension
questions.direct_answer: A `Runnable` describes a task separately from how it is scheduled. The same task can be run by a `Thread`, an executor, or another framework, and the class remains free to extend a meaningful superclass. Extending `Thread` is valid when customizing the thread object itself, but it mixes the task with its execution mechanism. A `Thread` also implements `Runnable`; do not say it cannot be submitted, although submitting a Thread calls its `run()` as a task and does not start that Thread object.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of object-oriented design principles and thread management best practices in production Java applications
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Simply stating 'Runnable is better' without explaining the single inheritance limitation or the task-thread separation principle
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that ExecutorService cannot accept Thread subclasses directly, demonstrating awareness of modern concurrent programming patterns

sections.title: Runnable vs Extending Thread, From the Ground Up
sections.content:
Both approaches give you a **background task** that runs on its own thread. With `extends Thread`, your class *is* a thread. With `implements Runnable`, your class is just the **task**, and a separate thread runs it.

That single difference decides almost everything. Java allows a class to extend only **one** parent. If you extend `Thread`, that inheritance slot is gone—your class can no longer extend a base service or a framework class.

**Runnable keeps the slot free.** You write the task once, then hand it to whatever runs it: a raw `Thread`, a scheduled job, or a thread pool.

Now the part interviewers push on: a thread pool. Modern apps run tasks through an **ExecutorService** (a managed pool that reuses threads). `ExecutorService` accepts `Runnable` and `Callable`—it does **not** accept `Thread` subclasses. So extending `Thread` locks you out of the standard concurrency toolkit.

> **Rule of thumb:** model the *task* with `Runnable`, not a *kind of thread* with `extends Thread`. That's composition over inheritance in one decision.

sections.title: Which One Should You Reach For?
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TD Q[Do you need to change
the thread itself?] -->|No, just run a task| R[Implement Runnable] Q -->|Yes, custom start/lifecycle| T[Extend Thread - rare] R --> P[Works with new Thread,
execute, and submit] R --> F[Inheritance slot stays free] T --> L[Inheritance slot used up] T --> X[Cannot go into a thread pool] ``` Nearly every real path lands on the left: implement Runnable.

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
blue|Runnable|~Describes a task|run() method|works with Thread and executors|class can still extend another class
emerald|Thread subclass|~Combines task and runner|inherits Thread lifecycle|still implements Runnable|use only when extending Thread itself matters
amber|Executor behavior|~Accepts Runnable|passing a Thread object is legal|executor calls run as a task|it does not call start()
violet|Design rule|~Separate work from mechanism|easier testing and reuse|executor owns scheduling|prefer composition for ordinary tasks

sections.title: Wrong: extending Thread burns the inheritance slot
Right: implement Runnable and let a pool run it
When to Choose Runnable
sections.content:
Use **Runnable** in virtually all production scenarios. In a Spring Boot service, background work—sending notifications, processing uploads, refreshing a cache—goes to an `ExecutorService` as `Runnable` tasks, and the pool manages the threads.

When your task class must extend a base class like `AbstractService` or a framework component, `Runnable` is your only option, since the inheritance slot stays open.

When you write a reusable task library, `Runnable` keeps the task independent of how it runs—a client can drive it with `Thread`, `ExecutorService`, or `CompletableFuture.runAsync`. The only time to extend `Thread` is to customise the thread's own behaviour, which is rare outside framework internals.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Saying an executor rejects Thread subclasses:** `Thread` implements `Runnable`, so it is accepted; the executor calls `run()` as a task rather than `start()`.
- **Claiming the two forms have different thread weight:** the execution mechanism determines the thread, not whether the task class extends Thread.
- **Calling `run()` and expecting concurrency:** a direct call runs on the current thread; `start()` creates the new Thread execution.
- **Extending Thread for ordinary work:** this couples the job to its runner and prevents extending another class.
- **Assuming Runnable always means a pool:** it only describes the task; a Thread, executor, or direct call can run it.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Single inheritance**: Extending `Thread` consumes the one `extends` slot; implementing `Runnable` leaves it free.
- **Task vs mechanism**: `Runnable` is the task; `Thread` and `ExecutorService` are ways to run it—separation of concerns.
- **Pool compatibility**: Thread pools accept `Runnable` and `Callable`, not `Thread` subclasses.
- **Composition over inheritance**: You compose thread behaviour instead of inheriting it—an OOP best practice.
- **Reusability**: The same `Runnable` can run on a raw thread, a pool, or `CompletableFuture`.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: Implementing Runnable is preferred over extending Thread for three reasons. First, Java doesn't support multiple inheritance. If you extend Thread, you can't extend any other class, which limits your design. In real apps you often need to extend a base service or a framework component. Second, Runnable separates the task from how it runs. You define what to do, not how to run it. So you can reuse the same task with a raw thread, a thread pool, or a scheduled executor. Third, and this is the one that stands out, an ExecutorService can't accept Thread subclasses. Its execute and submit methods only take Runnable or Callable. So extending Thread locks you out of modern concurrency utilities like thread pools. Most Spring Boot apps run background work, like sending emails or processing uploads, through an ExecutorService with Runnable tasks. It's cleaner and more flexible. The only time you'd extend Thread is to customize the thread's own behavior, like overriding start, which is rare outside framework internals.

questions.question: What is the difference between Runnable and Callable in Java?
questions.title: Runnable vs Callable in Java
questions.direct_answer: Runnable has a run method that returns void and cannot throw checked exceptions. Callable has a call method that returns a value of type V and can throw checked exceptions. Use Callable when you need a result from the task or need to propagate checked exceptions.

interviewer_intent.testing: Awareness of both concurrent task interfaces and ability to choose the right abstraction based on requirements
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing Callable can throw checked exceptions, which is a key advantage when tasks involve I/O or database operations
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Demonstrate the Future.get pattern for retrieving Callable results and explain how ExecutorService.submit returns Future for both

sections.title: Runnable vs Callable, From the Ground Up
sections.content:
Both are **interfaces for a task** that runs on a thread. The difference is what comes back when the task finishes.

**`Runnable`** came first (Java 1.0). Its method `run()` returns **void**—it just does work. It also **can't throw checked exceptions**, so anything like `IOException` must be caught inside `run()`. It's the fire-and-forget task.

**`Callable`** arrived in Java 5 to solve two gaps: a task that **returns a result**, and a task that **throws checked exceptions**. Its method `call()` returns a typed value `V` and declares `throws Exception`.

How do you read the result? You submit a `Callable` to an **ExecutorService** and get back a **Future**—a handle to a result that isn't ready yet. Call `future.get()` and it **blocks** until the value arrives.

> **Mental split:** `Runnable` is for side effects (send, log, clean up); `Callable` is for answers you need back (fetch, compute, validate).

sections.title: Submitting a Callable and Reading the Future
sections.content:
```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant M as Main thread
    participant E as ExecutorService
    participant W as Worker thread
    M->>E: submit(callable)
    E-->>M: returns Future now
    E->>W: run call() on a worker
    M->>M: do other work
    M->>E: future.get()
    Note over M: BLOCKS until ready
    W-->>E: result of call()
    E-->>M: get() returns the value
```

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Runnable|~run() returns void|no checked exceptions|execute() or Thread|fire-and-forget
blue|Callable|~call() returns a value|throws checked exc|submit() to a Future|read the result
emerald|Result|~How you read it|Runnable: side effects|Callable: Future.get()|blocks until done
violet|Pick|~Need a value?|yes - Callable|no - Runnable|both run in pools

sections.title: Runnable vs Callable Comparison
sections.content:
| Feature | Runnable | Callable |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Method Signature | void run() | V call() throws Exception |
| Return Value | No return value (void) | Returns result of type V |
| Exception Handling | Cannot throw checked exceptions | Can throw checked exceptions |
| Use with ExecutorService | execute() or submit() | Only submit() |
| Result Retrieval | No result available | Returns Future<V> for result |

sections.title: Runnable vs Callable in Action
When to Use Each Interface
sections.content:
Use **Runnable** for fire-and-forget tasks that don't produce a result: sending notifications, logging events, updating caches, triggering cleanup. If the task just performs an action, `Runnable` is simpler.

Use **Callable** when you need a computed result: fetching from an API, querying a database, processing a file and returning statistics. Also use `Callable` when the task naturally throws checked exceptions—`SQLException` for database work, `IOException` for file I/O.

The `Future` returned by `submit` lets you check completion with `isDone`, retrieve the value with `get`, or handle a failure: if `call()` threw, `future.get()` throws an `ExecutionException` wrapping it.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Forcing try-catch into Runnable**: Wrapping everything in `try-catch` inside `run()` when the task can fail signals you should be using `Callable` to propagate the exception.
- **Forgetting Future.get blocks**: `future.get()` blocks the calling thread until the result is ready. Calling it too early stalls the main thread on a slow task.
- **Using Runnable when a result is needed**: Stashing results in shared fields instead of returning them from `Callable` adds needless thread-safety risk.
- **Not knowing submit takes both**: `submit` accepts a `Runnable` too—it just returns a `Future` whose `get()` returns null after normal completion.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Return value**: `Runnable.run()` returns void; `Callable.call()` returns a typed result.
- **Exceptions**: `Callable` can throw checked exceptions; `Runnable` must catch them internally.
- **Future pattern**: `submit(callable)` returns `Future<V>`; `future.get()` blocks until ready.
- **Method names**: `Runnable` has `run()`, `Callable` has `call()`.
- **ExecutorService methods**: both work with `submit`; only `Runnable` works with `execute`.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: The main difference is what they return and how they handle exceptions. Runnable has a run method that returns void. It's for tasks that just do work without a result. It also can't throw checked exceptions, so an IOException has to be caught inside run. Callable has a call method that returns a value, whatever type you set with the generic parameter. And it can throw checked exceptions directly, which is great for database or file work. When you submit a Callable to an ExecutorService, you get back a Future. You call get on the Future to retrieve the result, and it blocks until the task finishes. If the task threw, Future.get throws an ExecutionException wrapping it. In practice, use Runnable for fire-and-forget tasks like sending emails or logging. Use Callable when you need a computed result, like fetching data from an API. The exception-handling difference is the one that stands out, so mention it if the task involves I/O or databases.

questions.question: What is ThreadLocal in Java and when would you use it?
questions.title: ThreadLocal in Java
questions.direct_answer: `ThreadLocal<T>` associates a separate value with each thread that accesses it; it does not copy one shared object automatically. It can hold request context in thread-per-request code, but values must be removed when threads are reused. Avoid using it as hidden global state or as a general way to manage database connections.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands per-thread state management, a pattern used extensively in Spring and Jakarta EE frameworks
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing that ThreadLocal values must be explicitly removed to avoid memory leaks, especially in thread pools where threads are reused
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention Spring's RequestContextHolder or SecurityContextHolder as production examples of ThreadLocal, showing awareness of framework internals

sections.title: ThreadLocal, From the Ground Up
sections.content:
**`ThreadLocal<T>`** provides a per-thread slot. Calling `get()` on two threads can return two different values, even though both use the same `ThreadLocal` object. The values are created or assigned separately; Java does not clone an initial object for every thread.

It can carry context through code that stays on one platform thread, such as a correlation ID in a traditional request pipeline. In a thread pool, the worker outlives the task, so call `remove()` in `finally` or a later task may inherit stale data. Thread-local context also does not automatically follow work moved to another thread or asynchronous stage.

Do not use `ThreadLocal` to hide ordinary method inputs or to own pooled database connections manually. Framework-managed transaction context may use it internally, but application code should follow the framework's lifecycle and prefer explicit context where practical.

sections.title: Two Threads, Two Isolated Values
sections.content:
```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant A as Thread A
    participant TL as ThreadLocal store
    participant B as Thread B
    A->>TL: set(user-1)
    B->>TL: set(user-2)
    A->>TL: get()
    TL-->>A: user-1
    B->>TL: get()
    TL-->>B: user-2
    Note over A,B: each thread sees only its own value
    A->>TL: remove() at request end
```

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|ThreadLocal|~Value associated with current thread|get/set/remove|different threads can see different values|not shared-value synchronization
blue|Suitable use|~Truly thread-scoped context|correlation or tenant id|legacy API adapter where needed|prefer explicit parameters when practical
emerald|Reuse risk|~Pool threads outlive tasks|old value may remain|set in narrow scope|remove in finally
violet|Boundary|~Does not follow work automatically|async handoff may use another thread|large values retain memory|document ownership

sections.title: Wrong: no remove() in a pooled thread
Right: set, use, then remove in a finally block
When to Use ThreadLocal
sections.content: Use `ThreadLocal` only for data whose lifetime and meaning genuinely belong to one thread, such as a correlation context managed by an established framework. Prefer explicit parameters for normal application dependencies because they remain clear across tests and asynchronous handoffs. For date and time formatting, prefer immutable `java.time` formatters rather than keeping `SimpleDateFormat` per thread. When a reused worker is involved, set the value for the narrowest scope and remove it in `finally`.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Forgetting cleanup on a reused worker:** a value can remain visible to a later task and retain referenced objects.
- **Assuming context follows asynchronous work:** a task may run on another thread, so propagation needs an explicit framework or wrapper.
- **Using it as hidden dependency injection:** implicit state makes code harder to reason about and test.
- **Using it for a shared value:** each thread gets its own association; it is not a replacement for synchronization.
- **Storing large or long-lived objects casually:** values live at least as long as their thread association remains.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Meaning**: one `ThreadLocal` key can map to a different value for each thread.
- **Not a copy mechanism**: mutable objects are not cloned automatically.
- **Pool hazard**: worker threads outlive tasks, so stale values can leak to later work.
- **Cleanup**: call `remove()` in `finally` when setting per-task context.
- **Boundary**: values do not automatically cross threads or asynchronous stages.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`ThreadLocal` associates a value with the current thread. Two threads calling `get()` on the same `ThreadLocal` can receive different values. It does not clone one object; each thread initializes or sets its own value.

A traditional request thread can use this for a correlation ID that many logging calls need. The important boundary is thread reuse. In a pool, the worker handles another task later, so I remove the value in `finally`. It also will not automatically follow a `CompletableFuture` onto another thread. I avoid using it as hidden application state or manually storing database connections; explicit parameters and framework-managed lifecycles are safer.

questions.question: How does the Runnable interface relate to lambda expressions?
questions.title: Runnable as a Functional Interface
questions.direct_answer: `Runnable` is a functional interface whose single abstract method is `void run()`. A no-argument, void-compatible lambda can target it, such as `() -> doWork()`. An expression statement may be void-compatible even if the called method returns a value, because that value can be ignored. Captured local variables must be final or effectively final.

interviewer_intent.testing: Connection between multithreading concepts and Java 8 functional programming features, showing breadth of knowledge
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not recognizing Runnable as a functional interface or not knowing that method references also work as Runnable implementations
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Demonstrate a lambda and method reference as Runnable, and mention the at-FunctionalInterface annotation validates this contract

sections.title: Runnable as a Functional Interface, From the Ground Up
sections.content:
A **functional interface** is an interface with exactly **one abstract method**. `Runnable` qualifies: its only method is `run()`, which takes no input and returns void.

That single-method shape matters because, since **Java 8**, a **lambda expression** can implement any functional interface. So any lambda with no parameters and no return value *is* a `Runnable`.

Why this helps: before Java 8, a small task meant a verbose **anonymous class**—`new Runnable() { public void run() { ... } }`. Now you write `() -> { ... }`, or even a **method reference** when the work already lives in a method.

The `@FunctionalInterface` annotation on `Runnable` documents the contract and makes the compiler enforce it—add a second abstract method and compilation fails.

> **The non-obvious edge:** a lambda can only read variables that are **effectively final**. Capturing a loop counter directly won't compile—copy it into a final local first.

sections.title: Three Ways to Supply a Runnable
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TD R[Runnable: one method, run] --> A[Anonymous class
verbose, pre-Java-8] R --> L[Lambda
arrow syntax, no name] R --> M[Method reference
existing no-arg void method] L --> E[executor.execute runs any of them] M --> E A --> E ```

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Functional Interface|~One abstract method|Runnable.run()|@FunctionalInterface|lambda-ready
blue|Lambda Form|~Concise|() arrow body|replaces anon class|since Java 8
emerald|Method Reference|~Even shorter|this::process|ClassName::method|when signature matches
violet|Benefit|~Less boilerplate|no anon-class noise|reads as a task|same Runnable type

sections.title: Wrong: capturing a loop variable directly
Right: lambdas and method references as Runnable
When to Use Lambdas for Runnable
sections.content:
Use a **lambda** for simple, one-off tasks that don't need reuse—`executor.execute(() -> cache.clear())` is cleaner than a whole `ClearCacheTask` class.

Use a **method reference** when the logic already exists as a method: `executor.execute(this::sendEmail)` reads better than `() -> sendEmail()`.

But when a task has complex logic, holds state, or is reused across the codebase, define a proper class implementing `Runnable`. A 30-line lambda is unreadable and hard to test. Keep lambdas to a few lines; promote anything bigger to a named class.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Not knowing method references work**: Writing `() -> this.doWork()` when `this::doWork` is cleaner—any no-arg void method is a valid `Runnable`.
- **Capturing mutable variables**: Lambdas can only read effectively final variables. `() -> count++` on a mutable `count` won't compile—use `AtomicInteger` or rethink the design.
- **Capturing a loop variable**: The loop counter isn't effectively final; copy it into a final local before capturing.
- **Overusing lambdas**: Stuffing heavy business logic into a lambda makes it unreadable and untestable—use a class.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Functional interface**: `Runnable` has exactly one abstract method, so a lambda can implement it.
- **Lambda syntax**: `() -> { ... }`—empty params, void return matches `run()`.
- **Method reference**: any no-arg void method works via `Class::method` or `instance::method`.
- **@FunctionalInterface**: makes the compiler enforce the single-method contract.
- **Effectively final**: lambdas can only read final or effectively final variables—no mutable captures.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: Runnable is a functional interface, which means it has exactly one abstract method, the run method. Since Java 8, functional interfaces can be implemented with lambda expressions or method references, which makes concurrent code much more concise. Before Java 8, passing a task to a thread meant writing new Runnable with an anonymous class and overriding run. Now you just use a lambda: empty parentheses, an arrow, then the body. Method references work too. If a method takes no parameters and returns void, you can pass it directly as a Runnable using the double colon syntax. This shows up everywhere in production code. When you submit tasks to an executor, you'll see lambdas all the time. The key insight is that Runnable's signature, no parameters and void return, matches what a no-arg lambda produces. One gotcha to mention: a lambda can only read variables that are effectively final, so capturing a loop counter directly fails to compile. You copy it into a final local first. The at-FunctionalInterface annotation keeps Runnable a single-method interface.

questions.question: Can a Runnable be passed to both Thread and ExecutorService?
questions.title: Runnable Compatibility with Thread and ExecutorService
questions.direct_answer: A `Runnable` can be given to a `Thread` and to `Executor.execute` or `submit`. `execute` returns no `Future`; an uncaught runtime exception is handled through the worker thread's uncaught-exception path. `submit` captures task failure in the returned `Future`, so it is observed when `get()` is called. Neither method should be described as silently swallowing every exception.

interviewer_intent.testing: Confirmation that the candidate understands Runnable's versatility and the abstraction between task definition and execution strategy
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing ExecutorService also accepts Runnable—thinking it only takes Callable, or not understanding the difference between execute and submit
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that ExecutorService.submit returns Future even for Runnable, and clarify when to use execute versus submit

sections.title: Runnable's Universal Compatibility, From the Ground Up
sections.content:
A `Runnable` describes a task through `void run()`. The same task can be passed to `new Thread(runnable)`, `Executor.execute(runnable)`, or `ExecutorService.submit(runnable)`. Calling `run()` directly is also legal but runs synchronously on the caller.

The runner decides the execution policy. `Thread.start()` schedules that Thread object's new execution. An executor invokes the Runnable on a worker chosen by its implementation; if the Runnable object also happens to be a Thread subclass, the executor still calls it as a task and does not call its `start()`.

`execute` returns no result handle. `submit` returns a Future: for an ordinary Runnable submission, `get()` returns null after normal completion and throws on cancellation or task failure. This separates task code from lifecycle, scheduling, and failure observation.

sections.title: One Runnable, Three Runners
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TD R[One Runnable task] --> T[new Thread then start
one-off thread, no pool] R --> E[execute on a pool
fire-and-forget, returns void] R --> S[submit on a pool
returns a Future] S --> G[get waits for completion
or surfaces an error] ```

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Runnable Everywhere|~One task type|new Thread(r)|executor.execute(r)|executor.submit(r)
blue|Thread|~Direct, low-level|manual lifecycle|no pooling|fine for learning
emerald|ExecutorService|~Managed pool|reuses threads|queues tasks|production choice
violet|Why It Matters|~Write once|swap Thread for a pool|no task rewrite|decoupled design

sections.title: Risky: exceptions from execute vanish
Better: submit returns a Future you can inspect
When to Use Thread vs ExecutorService
sections.content: A `Runnable` can be passed to either a `Thread` or an executor. A directly owned Thread can be reasonable for a dedicated lifecycle or a small demonstration. An executor is useful when an application needs task submission, scheduling policy, reusable platform workers, virtual-thread execution, results, cancellation, or coordinated shutdown. Choose a concrete executor and queue policy deliberately; the `ExecutorService` interface alone does not promise a fixed or bounded pool.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Saying execute hides every exception:** an uncaught failure follows the worker's uncaught-exception handling; the submitter simply receives no Future.
- **Ignoring a Future from submit:** task failures remain wrapped until code observes the Future.
- **Saying Future.get is always null:** it returns null only after normal completion of the usual Runnable submission; on failure or cancellation it throws.
- **Assuming every executor is a thread pool:** implementations include single-worker, scheduled, fork/join, and virtual-thread models.
- **Forgetting shutdown:** a component should stop an executor it owns according to its lifecycle.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Universal interface**: `Runnable` works with the `Thread` constructor and both `ExecutorService` methods.
- **Task vs execution**: `Runnable` defines the task; `Thread` and `ExecutorService` define how it runs.
- **execute vs submit**: `execute` is fire-and-forget; `submit` returns a `Future`.
- **Future for Runnable**: `submit(runnable)` returns a `Future<?>` that resolves to `null`.
- **Thread reuse**: a pool reuses threads; raw thread creation doesn't scale.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: Yes, absolutely. A Runnable can go to the Thread constructor and to ExecutorService methods like execute and submit. That's one of the key design strengths of Runnable. It separates the task from how it runs. You write the task once, then run it with a raw thread, with a pool, or submit it many times, without changing the task code. When you're learning, you might use new Thread with a Runnable and call start. But in production you'd almost always use an ExecutorService, because the pool reuses threads instead of creating a new one each time. ExecutorService has two main methods for a Runnable. Execute is fire-and-forget and returns nothing. Submit also accepts a Runnable, but it returns a Future. Future.get returns null after a Runnable completes normally, but it's still useful. You can call get to wait for completion, or check isDone, or catch an exception that happened during execution. One gotcha to mention: a failure from execute is not delivered through a Future and instead follows the worker's uncaught-exception handling, so use submit and check the future to see it. The same Runnable works everywhere, which is why it's a widely used task interface in Java.

familiarity_anchors: a universal charger for any device
a USB cable that fits many ports
a recipe that works on any stove
speakable_v2.hook: Write a Runnable once, then run it anywhere. A raw thread, a thread pool, even a plain method call. The task never changes.

beats.text: A Runnable is just the task. The thread is the worker that runs it, and a thread is the smallest unit of execution within a process. The same Runnable goes into a new Thread, into execute, or into submit.

That's exactly why a task that implements Runnable beats a class that extends Thread. Define the work once, then run it any way. Synchronous in a test, pooled in production, on one thread or hundreds.

items: A new Thread wraps the runnable, and start runs it. That's one thread, no pool.
execute on a pool is fire-and-forget. It hands back nothing.
submit on a pool returns a Future. That's how to wait or catch an error.

beats.text: Picture the order app starting on raw threads, then moving to a pool for scale. The Runnable code stays identical. Here's the non-obvious part. submit on a Runnable still returns a Future, but get returns null after normal completion. Its only use is to wait or surface a thrown error.

items: An exception inside a Runnable run by execute just vanishes. Use submit and check the Future.
Don't create raw threads in a web handler. An unbounded thread count will sink the service.

speakable_v2.cap: So one Runnable fits a raw thread and a pool alike. That's why it's the universal task in Java.
